question:
A 85-year-old female patient comes to the clinic with a one-month history of dull, localized low back
pain in the paraspinal region. The pain worsens with prolonged standing and forward bending. She
denies trauma, numbness, or weakness. Her past medical history is unremarkable. On examination,

muscle strength, tone, and reflexes in the lower extremities are normal, and sensation is intact. A
straight leg raise test produces moderate lumbar pain without radicular symptoms. Structural
examination reveals restricted lumbar flexion, pain at end range, and an anterior L5 tender point on the
left. Which of the following counterstrain treatment positions is most appropriate? Answer Choices: (A)
Hip flexed with left sidebending and right rotation (B) Hip extended with right sidebending and left
rotation (C) Hip flexed with right sidebending and left rotation (D) Hip flexed with no sidebending or
rotation (E) Hip flexed with bilateral sidebending and no rotation (F) Hip flexed with right sidebending
and right rotation (G) Hip extended with left sidebending and right rotation (H) Hip flexed with left
sidebending and left rotation (I) Hip flexed with minimal sidebending and contralateral rotation (J) Hip
extended with bilateral sidebending and ipsilateral rotation
 A. Hip extended with right sidebending and left rotation
B. Hip flexed with left sidebending and left rotation
C. Hip flexed with right sidebending and left rotation
D. Hip extended with bilateral sidebending and ipsilateral rotation
E. Hip flexed with left sidebending and right rotation
F. Hip extended with left sidebending and right rotation
G. Hip flexed with bilateral sidebending and no rotation
H. Hip flexed with no sidebending or rotation
I. Hip flexed with right sidebending and right rotation
J. Hip flexed with minimal sidebending and contralateral rotation
